title: Shrinking the binary: compiler and linker flags

videos.script: Lesson 1 built hits, and the binary came out at four megabytes. That is a lot for a program that counts lines. This lesson finds out where the bytes go, and which of them you can do without. {{sections}} First, a look inside the file. Tools that come with Linux and with Go list its sections and its symbols. Code is less than a third of it. Nearly as much is information for debuggers, which the program never reads. {{flags}} Then two linker flags remove that information, and the file loses a third of its size. A stripped binary still names every function in a stack trace, and you will see why. {{version}} Next, the binary learns to say which version it is. The go command records the git tag by itself. A linker flag fills in the name when there is no repository to read. {{further}} Then the levers beyond the linker: a compressor, a compiler flag, and the imports themselves. Only the imports move megabytes. {{podman}} Last, the lab gains a container runtime. Podman runs containers as an ordinary user, and lesson 18 needs it.
